new_statements.quote: 131. Stress. Stress in general carries a rather low functional load. [...] there are no examples of minimal lexical contrast involving stress as a distinctive feature. Nevertheless, it is generally true that: 1) Spanish loan words occur with primary stress on the originally stressed syllable, i.e., usually the penult [...] 2) a few morphemes are inherently stressed [...] 3) and, in the remaining cases, that is, the great majority, the first syllable of a morphological word (see Sec. 320) commonly occurs with primary stress [...] Thus, it would appear that primary stress is morphologically predictable.
new_statements.citation: Ultan, Russell. 1967. Konkow Grammar. Ph.D. dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. Chapter One (Phonology), Sec. 130 Suprasegmentals and Sec. 131 Stress, pp. 24-26; Sec. 260 Stress, p. 46.
new_statements.locator: Sec. 131, pp. 25-26 (PDF pp. 33-34 of the eScholarship scan); Sec. 260, p. 46 (PDF p. 51). Page images of pp. 25, 26, 46 checked by eye against the scanned.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (200 pp., image-only; dissertation page N = PDF page N+8) and rendered PDF pp. 1-2, 9-11, 33, 34, 51 to PNG to read by eye. Sec. 131 'Stress' begins on diss. p. 25 (PDF p. 33) and the quoted passage is there verbatim: 'Stress in general carries a rather low functional load. Contrastive stress has been noted in a small number of utterances... but there are no examples of minimal lexical contrast involving stress as a distinctive feature. Nevertheless, it is generally true that: 1) Spanish loan words occur with primary stress on the originally stressed syllable, i.e., usually the penult: wàké·nu 'cowboy' (< vaquero)... 2) a few morphemes are inherently stressed: kàwácu 'madrone'... 3)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the morphological word in the great majority of native words; Ultan calls primary stress 'morphologically predictable'. He nevertheless posits two stress phonemes (primary and secondary, weak unmarked) because of exceptions: Spanish loans keep their original (usually penultimate) stress with a drift toward native initial stress, a few morphemes are inherently stressed, and there is English-influenced free variation (e.g. pélepèle ~ pèlepéle 'ankle'). Stress is not lexically contrastive (no minimal pairs); contrastive stress occurs in a few utterances. Sec. 140 adds that every syllable carries some degree of stress (primary, secondary or weak).
new_statements.secondary_stress: A secondary stress phoneme is posited (p. 26: 'Secondary stress consists of strong amplitude and low to mid pitch'; primary = strong to extra-strong amplitude with mid-to-high pitch; weak = weak amplitude, low-to-mid pitch). No placement rule for secondary stress is given; examples show it on non-initial syllables (e.g. kàwácu 'madrone', kàpó·ta ~ kápo·ta 'coat').
new_statements.exceptions: (1) Spanish loans stressed on the originally stressed syllable, usually the penult (wàké·nu 'cowboy' < vaquero), with variants showing assimilation to initial stress (kàpó·ta ~ kápo·ta 'coat', sòmlé·lo ~ sómle·lo 'hat'); (2) inherently stressed morphemes (kàwácu 'madrone', pýpin vs. wypýpin 'come loose' vs. tápin, wítapin 'squeeze'); (3) considerable variation attributed to English influence (bómyhmỳhnotin ~ bòmyhmýhnotin 'cause to feel sad', pélepèle ~ pèlepéle 'ankle', lóskopdi ~ lòskópdi 'in the mud'); (4) Sec. 260 p. 46: 'there are many examples in which the pattern deviates from the expected norm in at present unpredictable fashion. Pending more exhaustive analysis, I cannot formulate rules to account for the divergent cases.'
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the morphological word (Sec. 320: a word = minor-class word or a construction with inflectional suffix(es); clitics attach without juncture). Sec. 260 p. 46: 'Words tend to retain the same relative stress pattern which they exhibit as citation forms in most environments.' Examples are whole inflected verb words (sóldojcodèno 'Did you begin to sing long ago?', pínehwònomàncodè 'He must have brought lunch, mustn't he?'). Stress is marked phonemically on every form cited in the grammar.
new_statements.identity_note: Ultan's 'Konkow' is Northwest(ern) Maidu = nort2951 (ISO mjd); he adopts Shipley's term Konkow explicitly to separate it from Maidu (Northeastern Maidu, maid1262) and Nisenan (nise1244). The description rests on three principal speakers from Bean Creek, Cherokee and Bald Rock (Feather River drainage, Butte County), fieldwork 1961-1964, with minor idiolectal/regional differences noted. The CLA page dates the dissertation 1961 (Ultan's A.B. date); the eScholarship record and title page give 1967.

sources.note: Ch. 1 Sec. 130-131 (pp. 24-26): two stress phonemes (primary, secondary) posited; stress has low functional load, no minimal lexical pairs; in the great majority of words the first syllable of the morphological word carries primary stress, so primary stress is 'morphologically predictable'; Spanish loans keep original (usually penult) stress; a few inherently stressed morphemes; English-influenced variation. Sec. 260 (p. 46): words keep their citation-form stress pattern in most environments; many deviations not yet rule-governed.
